name: Felix Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a lead hand for a general contractor that mostly builds public stuff: schools, health clinics, a library last year. Right now it's a primary school extension, six classrooms, and my team of seven does the interior: metal stud walls, plasterboard, door frames, ceilings. I'm in at seven, go through the day with the site manager, then I'm moving between rooms checking lines and sorting out whoever's stuck. I like that the buildings are for kids and nurses, it feels decent; the bit I can't stand is when the electricians and us are fighting over the same wall on the same day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Ama, my girlfriend, she's training to be an accountant and studies most evenings. We're getting married in about eighteen months, so we're saving for that and trying not to let her mum invite four hundred people. I use an AI app sometimes, mostly to check a building regulation or work out a quantity when I'm not sure, but I'm not glued to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. We call it AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was useful for some things and overhyped for most. I'd probably say it at lunch and leave it there. Ama's office would be the one that notices, not mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the plan stays the plan: wedding, then save for a house, then maybe run my own small team in a few years. My work wasn't really in the firing line in the first place. So, mostly relief.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, keep saving for the wedding, and keep using the app when it helps. I'd probably sign up for the supervisor course my company offers next year, because that's the next step whether AI's a big deal or not. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a forecast for rain that doesn't come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Ama, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be fine too, I think. They say AI was going to wipe out accountants, and if it doesn't, she's got a good career ahead. That matters to me as much as my own job, honestly, because she's the steadier earner long term.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd do differently if you knew for sure this was coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe stop reading those articles on my break. And I'd feel better about locking in a mortgage after the wedding instead of waiting.

S0.say: I'd say it was useful for some things and overhyped for most, at lunch, and leave it there. Ama's office would notice more than mine.
S0.think: For me the plan stays the plan: wedding, then a house, then maybe running my own team. My work was never really in the firing line, so it's mostly relief.
S0.do: Keeps working, saving for the wedding and using the AI app when it helps. Signs up for his company's supervisor course next year and feels ready to lock in a mortgage after the wedding.
S0.feel: Calm, like a forecast for rain that never comes.
S0.quote: That matters to me as much as my own job, honestly, because she's the steadier earner long term.
S0.fieldNote: Practical and future-planned around the wedding and a house. He measures the scenario partly through his fiancée's career. Nothing in this picture troubles him beyond some wasted worry on his breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a change we'll have to manage, and that firms and government both need to chip in for training. I don't think it's anyone's fault, it's just how things go. I'd say it to the lads and leave politics to others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit worried about my bit of the trade. I've seen videos of robots that hang plasterboard and spray finish ceilings, and that's literally what my team does all day. Carpenters who do fiddly work will be fine longer than us drywall guys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch which contractors start using the robots and how it goes. If it works, I'd ask my boss to train me to supervise them, because if someone's running a robot on site I'd rather it was me. I'd also put a bit more aside each month, maybe push the house plan back a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, but it would nag at me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kofi and Dmitri, they're my best boarders, fast and neat, but that's all they do. If a robot can hang a board, what's left for them is the awkward corners. I'd try to get them onto the ceilings and the finishing, the parts robots are worse at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd push the house back. Does Ama know you think like that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not yet, because we haven't had to talk about it. She'd say I'm overthinking, and she might be right. But I'd rather have the money and not need it.

S1.say: I'd say it's a change we'll have to manage and that firms and government should both chip in for training. It's nobody's fault; I'd say it to the lads and leave politics to others.
S1.think: Privately I'd worry about my bit of the trade, because robots that hang plasterboard and spray ceilings do exactly what my team does. Fiddly carpentry lasts longer than drywall.
S1.do: Watches which contractors adopt drywall robots and, if they work, asks to be trained to supervise them. Saves a bit more each month and considers pushing the house purchase back a year.
S1.feel: Uneasy, a nagging worry rather than fear, with concern for his two best boarders.
S1.quote: I've seen videos of robots that hang plasterboard and spray finish ceilings, and that's literally what my team does all day.
S1.fieldNote: He sees the steady scenario as a specific threat to drywall work, not carpentry in general. He'd adopt once proven, from the supervising side. He hasn't shared his cautious money thinking with his fiancée yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government has to do something fast, some kind of income support, and the companies making money from it should pay their share. I don't want everyone fighting, I want a plan. I'd probably say more online than usual, just sharing things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be scared stiff. The wedding's in eighteen months, the money's sitting in an account, and suddenly I'd be wondering whether we should spend it on a party or keep it to live on. And if AI can do accounting too, Ama's career goes at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, Ama and I would sit down and scale the wedding right back, maybe to the registry office and dinner with family. That saved money becomes the cushion. I'd look hard for any job on robot installation or site supervision while they still need people, even if it means a longer commute. I'd cut everything else, the car payment, the football season ticket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the scaffold moving when you're on the top lift. Your whole body goes tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ama's mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha, that's the scariest part. I'd tell her we're doing it small and putting the money towards our future, and she'd be upset, but she lived through hard times herself. I think she'd get it in the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years, is there any training you'd try?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a short robot operator course if one existed, because that's a few months, not years. I wouldn't start anything long, there's no point. I'd want work I can do right now while it lasts.

S2.say: I'd say the government must act fast with income support, and companies profiting should pay their share. I want a plan, not everyone fighting, and I'd share more things online than usual.
S2.think: Off the record I'd be scared stiff: the wedding money is sitting there and I'd wonder whether to spend it on a party or live on it. If AI can do accounting too, Ama's career goes at the same time.
S2.do: Scales the wedding back to a registry office and family dinner and keeps the money as a cushion. Cuts the car payment and football season ticket, and hunts for robot installation or supervision work, maybe via a short operator course, even with a longer commute.
S2.feel: Scared stiff, like a scaffold moving under him on the top lift.
S2.quote: I'd be wondering whether we should spend it on a party or keep it to live on.
S2.fieldNote: The wedding is the pressure point: the fast picture turns celebration money into survival money. He fears for both incomes at once. Pragmatic to the end, he'd only take training measured in months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if we start now. Companies and governments should be planning training and some safety net. I'd say it calmly, because panic doesn't help anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd see it as a ticking clock but one I can work with. I'd want to be out of plasterboard and into managing jobs before the robots arrive. Someone still has to coordinate the trades and deal with the client, at least for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the supervisor course in the first year, then a construction management diploma part-time, maybe two years. We'd still have the wedding, but smaller, and we'd hold off on the house until we see what happens around 2029. I'd try to get on the first project my company runs with robots, so I'm the one who knows how it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel like I'm doing something. That helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time change compared to two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the difference between running out of a burning building and walking out with your stuff. With five years I can finish a diploma. With two I'd just grab whatever job's going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't site managers be replaced too by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, in the end. But I think the people managing the robots and the clients go later than the people hanging boards. I'd rather be in the last group out than the first.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if we start now, with companies and government planning training and a safety net. I'd say it calmly, because panic helps no one.
S3.think: Privately it's a ticking clock I can work with: I want to be out of plasterboard and into managing jobs before the robots arrive. Someone still coordinates trades and clients for a while.
S3.do: Starts the supervisor course in the first year, then a two-year part-time construction management diploma. Keeps a smaller wedding, holds off on the house until around 2029 and tries to join his company's first robot project.
S3.feel: Anxious but feeling better for doing something.
S3.quote: It's the difference between running out of a burning building and walking out with your stuff.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives him a staged plan up and out of drywall. He admits management is exposed too but aims to be in the last group out. Still trimming the wedding and delaying the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning and we've got no excuse not to prepare. People my age need to plan their careers around it. I'd say that to the younger lads on site especially.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be all right for most of it. By 2036 I'd hope to be running jobs, with a house mostly sorted and maybe a kid. It would still hit, but I'd be standing on firmer ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the supervisor course and the diploma, have the wedding we planned, and buy a house a couple of years after with a mortgage we could pay on one income. I'd start using the AI tools more properly once the company rolls them out, so I'm comfortable with them by 2030. Maybe I'd put a bit into a pension or index fund too, so there's something working for us besides our jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not lying awake. Ten years is a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a mortgage you could pay on one income. Why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if one of us goes, the other can hold the house. Ama could be hit as hard as me in the end. It's just a sensible rule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the younger lads?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get your trade, but don't stop there. Learn to run a job, learn the computer side, and save something every month. Ten years goes quicker than you think, my dad always said that about everything.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is fair warning and there's no excuse not to prepare; people my age must plan careers around it. I'd say that to the younger lads on site especially.
S4.think: Off the record I'd be all right for most of it, hoping by 2036 to be running jobs with a house mostly sorted and maybe a child. It would still hit, but I'd be on firmer ground.
S4.do: Completes the supervisor course and diploma, has the planned wedding and buys a house a couple of years later with a mortgage payable on one income. Learns the company's AI tools by about 2030 and starts putting money into a pension or index fund.
S4.feel: Uneasy but not lying awake, since ten years feels long.
S4.quote: Because if one of us goes, the other can hold the house.
S4.fieldNote: The decade lets him keep almost all his life plans while building in safety margins, like a one-income mortgage. He'd adopt the tools as they roll out, true to his steady profile. Calmest of his AGI answers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because of the timing with the wedding and Ama's job. What would help is some kind of steady income from the government while people retrain, and short courses that actually lead to work. Something practical, not promises.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the buildings. If robots build schools faster and cheaper, maybe kids get better schools sooner. I'd like to think something good comes out of it, even if it's not good for me.

headlineQuote: If robots build schools faster and cheaper, maybe kids get better schools sooner.
portrait: Felix is a 27-year-old lead hand running interior fit-out on public buildings like schools and clinics, engaged to Ama, a trainee accountant, with a wedding eighteen months away. He uses AI now and then and adopts new things once proven. He is calm in the plateau, uneasy in steady disruption because drywall robots do exactly what his team does, and alarmed by fast AGI, which turns wedding money into survival money. With five or ten years he plans a route into site management and builds safety margins into the wedding and the mortgage. He blames no one and wants practical help from both firms and government.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would land around the wedding and could hit his and Ama's jobs at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: A steady government income while people retrain, and short courses that actually lead to work.
